name: Anki
tagline: Spaced repetition flashcard app with cross-device sync and a huge library of community decks.

pricing.basis: one-time purchase, desktop and Android are free
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The scheduler is not the hard part: FSRS is published, there are open source implementations, and a local card store plus a review queue is an afternoon of work. An agent can absolutely give you a personal flashcard app that reviews cards in a sane order and never loses your history. What it cannot hand you in one session is the part people actually lean on: a polished offline mobile client, conflict-safe sync between phone and laptop, and the thousands of community decks that make medical school and language learning tolerable. If you write your own cards and study on one device, a DIY build is genuinely fine. If you were planning to download a 30,000 card shared deck and study it on the train, you are rebuilding infrastructure, not an app.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you add cards, and it schedules reviews with FSRS and tracks your streak and backlog.
requirements: somewhere to run it locally or on a small box you control
willingness to write your own cards or import CSV
whatYouLose: The shared deck library, which is most of Anki's practical value for students
AnkiMobile and AnkiDroid: real offline mobile clients with sync that handles conflicts
The add-on ecosystem: image occlusion, cloze variants, heatmaps, TTS hooks
FSRS parameter optimization fit to your own review history rather than defaults
Decades of edge case handling in scheduling, leeches, burying and sibling cards
moatNotes: The deck ecosystem is a two sided thing: people share decks because everyone uses Anki, and everyone uses Anki because the decks are there.
whyPeopleStillPay: Mostly they do not, which is the funny part: the desktop app and AnkiWeb sync are free, and the money changes hands once for the iOS client. People pay that because reviewing on a phone in dead time is the entire reason spaced repetition works as a habit, and because their deck collection and multi year review history already live in the format. Paying once for the thing that makes the habit portable is a better deal than any weekend build.
notes: Rebuilding the scheduler is easy and slightly fun. Rebuilding the reason you open it on the bus is not.
prompt:
Build a local spaced repetition flashcard app. Single user, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud.

Stack, non negotiable:
- TypeScript everywhere.
- Backend: Node 20 with Hono, SQLite via better-sqlite3, migrations as plain .sql files applied on boot.
- Scheduling: the ts-fsrs package. Do not hand roll an algorithm.
- Frontend: Vite + React + Tailwind, served by the same process in production.
- One command to run: npm run dev. One command to build: npm run build.

Data model:
- decks (id, name, created_at)
- notes (id, deck_id, front markdown, back markdown, tags)
- cards (id, note_id, fsrs state blob, due, reps, lapses, suspended)
- reviews (id, card_id, rating, reviewed_at, elapsed_ms) append only, never deleted

Features in scope:
- Add, edit, delete notes with markdown and inline images stored on disk under ./data/media.
- Review screen: show front, reveal back on space, rate Again/Hard/Good/Easy with keys 1-4, FSRS decides next due.
- Daily queue with configurable new card and review limits per deck.
- Suspend and bury a card, plus a leech flag after N lapses.
- CSV import and export (front, back, tags) and a full JSON backup/restore.
- Stats page: reviews per day for 90 days, due forecast for 30 days, retention rate.
- Keyboard first, responsive layout that is usable on a phone browser. Add a service worker so it loads offline against a local server.

Explicitly out of scope: .apkg import, multi device sync, user auth, shared deck browsing, audio recording, add-on system. Do not stub them with fake buttons.

Store config in .env (PORT, DATA_DIR) with a committed .env.example. Write a README with setup, keybindings, and exactly how to back up the SQLite file. Include vitest tests for the queue builder and the CSV round trip.
